For linear S.H.M. the speed at displacement \( x \) is \( v = \omega \sqrt{A^{2} - x^{2}} \), and the maximum speed (at the mean position) is \( v_{\max} = \omega A \).

Put \( v = \dfrac{v_{\max}}{2} \):

\( \omega \sqrt{A^{2} - x^{2}} = \dfrac{\omega A}{2} \)

Squaring and cancelling \( \omega^{2} \):

\( A^{2} - x^{2} = \dfrac{A^{2}}{4} \quad \Rightarrow \quad x^{2} = \dfrac{3A^{2}}{4} \quad \Rightarrow \quad x = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} A \)

Note that the time period \( T \) is not needed — the speed-displacement relation is independent of it.

Why the others fail: \( \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} A \approx 1.15 A \) is larger than the amplitude, so the particle can never reach it. At \( x = A/2 \) the speed is \( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} v_{\max} \approx 0.87 v_{\max} \), not half. At \( x = \dfrac{A}{\sqrt{2}} \) the speed is \( \dfrac{v_{\max}}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.71 v_{\max} \) — that is the point where kinetic and potential energies are equal, a different condition.

Compare \( x = 6 \sin(100t + \pi/4) \) with \( x = A \sin(\omega t + \phi) \).

The displacement is given in centimetres, so the amplitude must be converted to SI units:

\( A = 6 \text{ cm} = 0.06 \text{ m}, \qquad \omega = 100 \text{ rad/s}, \qquad m = 1 \text{ kg} \)

The kinetic energy is maximum at the mean position, where the speed is \( v_{\max} = \omega A = 100 \times 0.06 = 6 \text{ m/s} \).

\( (K.E.)_{\max} = \dfrac{1}{2} m v_{\max}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} A^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1 \times (100)^{2} \times (0.06)^{2} \)

\( = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10000 \times 0.0036 = 18 \text{ J} \)

Why the others fail: \( 36 \) J is what you get by dropping the factor \( \dfrac{1}{2} \), i.e. computing \( m \omega^{2} A^{2} \). \( 9 \) J and \( 27 \) J do not follow from the given data at all. (Leaving the amplitude in centimetres gives an absurd \( 1.8 \times 10^{5} \) J, which is the unit trap this question is built around.)

A second's pendulum is *defined* by its period: \( T = 2 \) s, wherever it is. So the period must be the same on the moon as on the earth.

For a simple pendulum \( T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}} \), so \( L = \dfrac{g T^{2}}{4\pi^{2}} \).

With \( T \) fixed, \( L \propto g \). Hence

\( \dfrac{L_{m}}{L_{e}} = \dfrac{g_{m}}{g_{e}} = \dfrac{1}{6} \)

\( L_{m} = \dfrac{1}{6} \times 1 = \dfrac{1}{6} \text{ m} \approx 0.17 \text{ m} \)

Physically: gravity on the moon is weaker, so the bob is restored more slowly; the pendulum must be made *shorter* to keep the same 2-second beat.

Why the others fail: \( 6 \) m would follow if \( g \) on the moon were six times larger, not smaller. \( \dfrac{1}{36} \) m assumes \( L \propto g^{2} \), and \( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \) m assumes \( L \propto \sqrt{g} \); the relation is linear in \( g \).

For a mass \( m \) on a spring combination of effective constant \( k_{\text{eff}} \), the frequency is \( n = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{k_{\text{eff}}}{m}} \), so \( n \propto \sqrt{k_{\text{eff}}} \).

Two identical springs of constant \( k \):

**Series:** \( \dfrac{1}{k_{s}} = \dfrac{1}{k} + \dfrac{1}{k} = \dfrac{2}{k} \quad \Rightarrow \quad k_{s} = \dfrac{k}{2} \)

**Parallel:** \( k_{p} = k + k = 2k \)

Therefore

\( \dfrac{n_{s}}{n_{p}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{k_{s}}{k_{p}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{k/2}{2k}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \)

So \( n_{s} : n_{p} = 1 : 2 \) — the series combination is the softer (more easily stretched) one and therefore oscillates at the lower frequency.

Why the others fail: \( 1:4 \) is the ratio of the spring constants \( k_{s} : k_{p} \), not of the frequencies — the square root has been forgotten. \( 2:1 \) and \( 4:1 \) are these two ratios written the other way round, i.e. parallel-to-series, whereas the question asks for series first.

The graph starts at \( x = 0 \) and rises, so \( x = A \sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{T}\right) \).

For S.H.M. the restoring force is \( F = -m\omega^{2} x \), so \( |F| \) (and \( |a| \)) is largest where \( |x| \) is largest — at the extreme positions — and zero at the mean position, where instead the speed is largest.

Reading the graph at the marked instants:

- \( t = T/4 \): \( x = +A \) (positive extreme) — velocity zero, so \( K.E. = 0 \) and all the energy is potential.
- \( t = T/2 \): \( x = 0 \) (mean position) — speed is *maximum*, not zero.
- \( t = 3T/4 \): \( x = -A \) (negative extreme) — \( |x| \) is maximum, so \( |F| = m\omega^{2} A \) is **maximum**.
- \( t = T \): \( x = 0 \) (mean position) — acceleration \( = -\omega^{2} x = 0 \), i.e. minimum, not maximum.

Hence only the statement about the force at \( t = 3T/4 \) is correct.

Why the others fail: the acceleration at \( t = T \) is zero (option A); the velocity at \( t = T/2 \) is maximum, not zero (option C); and at \( t = T/4 \) the particle is momentarily at rest, so the kinetic energy is zero while the *potential* energy equals the total energy (option D).
